lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Set up repo and rebase cleanly
steps.instructions: In the empty workdir run `git init`, create and commit a file on main, then `git switch -c feature/login` and commit a change there. Switch back to main, commit a change to a different file, switch to `feature/login`, run `git rebase main`, then run `git log --oneline --graph --all` to see the linear history.

targets.caption: The feature commits are replayed on top of main

explanations.topic: Rebase sets commits aside and reapplies them on the latest main
Why it's called rebasing: new base commit

hints: Run git rebase main while you are on the feature branch, not on main.
The commit on main must touch a different file from the one on feature/login, otherwise you'll get a conflict.
Check which branch you are on with git status before you rebase.
Use git log --oneline --graph --all to confirm the feature commit now comes after main's latest commit.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase main while still on main, which does nothing.
Editing the same file on both branches, which causes a conflict in this step.
Forgetting to git add before committing, so the commit fails with 'nothing to commit'.
Not making any commit on main before creating the branch, so main has no history to branch from.
steps.code:
git init
git add . && git commit -m "initial commit"
git switch -c feature/login
git commit -am "feature work"
git switch main
git commit -am "main change"
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
git log --oneline --graph --all

steps.title: Check branch isn't pushed
steps.instructions: Run `git branch -a` to list local and remote branches. Confirm your feature branch has no `remotes/` entry, which means it is safe to rebase.

targets.caption: The branch list has no remotes/ entry for the feature branch

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so local and remote no longer match
git merge keeps hashes the same and never rewrites history
Use git branch -a to see whether the feature branch exists on the remote

hints: Use the git branch command with a flag that also shows remote branches.
In the output, look for a line like `remotes/origin/<your-feature-branch>`. If there isn't one, the branch hasn't been pushed and is safe to rebase.
common_mistakes: Running plain `git branch`, which shows only local branches and so can't tell you whether the feature branch was pushed.
Seeing `remotes/origin/<feature>` and rebasing anyway, which rewrites hashes that teammates may already have pulled.
Running the command outside the repository folder and getting `fatal: not a git repository`.
Assuming a branch is unpushed without running `git fetch` first when the remote branch list may be out of date.

steps.title: Create conflicts and start rebase
steps.instructions: Make three commits on `feature/login`: the first and third edit the same lines that two new commits on main also change, and the second touches an unrelated file. Run `git rebase main`, then `git status` to see the paused rebase.

targets.caption: The first feature commit conflicts with main
git status shows the rebase is paused

explanations.topic: Rebase reapplies feature commits one by one, so each can conflict
Feature branch's base commit vs. two newer commits on main
Rebase pauses on conflict; status shows which commit and how many remain
Fixing rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts

hints: Make sure main has new commits that edit the same lines as your feature commits, otherwise the rebase finishes cleanly.
Check out your feature branch before running `git rebase main`.
After the conflict appears, run `git status` to see 'rebase in progress' and the unmerged file.
Look for the 'Last command done' and 'Next commands to do' lines in the status output. They show the remaining commits.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while on main instead of the feature branch.
Making the conflicting edits on different lines, so Git auto-merges and no conflict appears.
Forgetting to commit the changes on main before rebasing.
Panicking and running `git rebase --abort` before inspecting `git status`.

steps.title: Resolve conflict and continue
steps.instructions: Open the conflicted file, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers while keeping the correct code, then `git add` the file. Run `git rebase --continue`, and in Vim press Esc and type `:wq` to keep the commit message.

precision_checks.label: No unmerged files
precision_checks.command: test -z "$(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U)" || git status | grep -q 'could not apply'

targets.caption: Remove the conflict markers and keep the correct code
Continue the rebase instead of committing

explanations.topic: Rebase uses git rebase --continue instead of commit
Saving and quitting Vim with :wq keeps the commit message

hints: Open each file listed as conflicted (git status shows 'both modified').
Delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, keeping only the code that should stay, then save.
Run git add on every fixed file, then git rebase --continue.
When Vim opens, press Escape, type :wq and press Enter.
common_mistakes: Leaving a conflict marker line (e.g. =======) in the file.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
Forgetting to git add the resolved file before continuing.
Getting stuck in Vim by typing :wq without pressing Escape first, or typing into insert mode.
steps.code:
git add <conflicted-file>
git rebase --continue
# in Vim: Esc, then :wq

steps.title: Finish the rebase
steps.instructions: Resolve the conflict in the last commit the same way, `git add` the file and run `git rebase --continue` again. Then run `git status` to confirm you are no longer rebasing.

targets.caption: git status shows a normal, clean branch

explanations.topic: Last commit conflicts again; resolve and continue
Using git status to confirm the rebase is over

hints: After the middle commit applies on its own, Git stops again at the last commit. Fix that conflict the same way you fixed the first one.
Open the conflicting file and remove every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> marker. Keep the content you want.
Stage the file with git add <file>, then run git rebase --continue. Save and close the commit message editor.
Run git status. It should say 'On branch ...' and should no longer mention a rebase in progress.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase --continue before running git add on the resolved file.
Leaving conflict markers in the file, then staging and committing them.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue during the rebase.
Not closing the commit message editor (e.g. Vim :wq), so the rebase never continues.
Running git rebase --skip by accident, which drops the last commit.
steps.code:
# resolve the conflict markers in the conflicting file, then:
git add <conflicting-file>
git rebase --continue
git status
